How we got here

Five months, from one problem to hundreds

How sure is anyone?

Claimed is not the same as proven

A math result is trusted when it is checked. Two kinds of checkers exist: a Lean computer check of every step, and human experts who read it. Each claim gets a meter below.

Touch a real problem

Erdős's dots: how many pairs are exactly 1 apart?

Place n dots on a flat page. Count every pair that is exactly 1 unit apart. In 1946 Erdős guessed that grid-like patterns are close to the best you can do. In May 2026 an OpenAI model showed that guess was wrong, with patterns built from algebraic number theory. Try the two simple patterns yourself.

unit pairs now0
pairs per dot0
square grid0
triangle grid0

Notice: the triangle grid beats the square grid. Both stay near 2–3 pairs per dot. The AI's patterns grow faster than any grid as n gets huge. That is why experts called it a real discovery.

Touch the $1M problem

Navier–Stokes: can a fluid's speed reach infinity?

One equation describes every liquid and gas: weather, wings, blood, smoke. The Millennium Prize question is whether its smooth solutions can suddenly blow up, with speed going to infinity at one point. OpenAI claims yes, when a smooth force keeps pushing. Drag to stir. Then press Squeeze.

+ = + + ,

drag to stir · bright = fast
peak speed0
× start of squeeze–
peak speed over time
squeeze radius: –

What you just saw, and what you can't see

The squeeze pushes a swirl into a smaller and smaller spot, so the peak speed climbs. Thick fluid (high ν) fights back and smooths it out. That tug-of-war, self-transport against viscosity, is the whole problem. A computer can never show infinity: the grid cells set a floor on how small the spot gets. Whether the true equations reach infinity in finite time can only be settled by a proof. OpenAI's claimed proof covers the case with a smooth push f. The force-free case is still open, and the Clay Institute lists the problem as active.

How a computer checks a proof

Be the Lean checker

Lean refuses any step that does not follow from earlier steps. That is why a Lean-checked proof can be trusted even if an AI wrote it. Run the check, then plant a mistake and watch it get caught.

What it means for people

  
The slow part of science just moved

  
For centuries, finding a proof was the slow, rare part. If an average result costs about three hours of compute, finding stops being the bottleneck. Checking, understanding and using become the hard part. Pick a horizon.

What nobody knows yet

  

    
?Whether the 245 results without a Lean-checked main proof are all correct. OpenAI's own notes say some may have problems.

    
?Whether the Navier–Stokes blow-up proof holds. The Clay Institute still lists the problem as open, and a credit dispute continues.

    
?How many attempts failed. OpenAI posed about 4,000 problems and has not said how the rest went.

    
?Who can check the work. The model is unreleased, so nobody outside OpenAI can rerun it.
